statement.es: Leer en voz alta cualquier palabra en hiragana, sin romaji en pantalla

note.en: Tofugu reports a day to a week. Four hours is the optimistic end of that and it is a real number, not encouragement.

unlocks.en: every other row, because every row is one consonant plus one of these five
unlocks.es: todas las demás filas, porque cada fila es una consonante más una de estas cinco

title.en: Five sounds, and everything else is built from them

en: Japanese has five vowel sounds and they do not change. a as in father, i as in machine, u as in flute, e as in bet, o as in for.
Every other kana in the table is one consonant plus one of these five, in that order, always. Learn the five and you have learned the second half of forty more.

title.en: Why this order and not the common ones first

en: This is gojuon order, the order the table itself is in, five to a row. No guide in the research recommended frequency order for kana and no study was found comparing the two.

The reason to keep gojuon is that dakuten, yoon and the whole romanisation system are column rules. Column order is therefore the rule-teaching order, and shuffling forty-six items by frequency throws that structure away to save nothing.

caption.en: a, three strokes. Stroke order is shown throughout this Book and graded nowhere in it.

title.en: k, s and t, and the three cells that lie

unlocks.en: most of the words you will meet first, and the habit of reading a row rather than a character

en: The k row is regular: ka ki ku ke ko.
The s row is not. The i cell is shi, not si. The t row breaks twice: the i cell is chi and the u cell is tsu.

Those three are the reason romaji arguments exist, and they are also the reason chapter 0 spent its time on beats. Japanese tu is physically tsu, which is why a stranded t in a foreign word takes an o instead.

title.en: Type the t row, including the two that lie

unlocks.en: the h row, which is where the b and p rows come from later

en: The n and m rows are regular. The h row breaks once: the u cell is fu, and the sound is neither an English f nor an English h but a breath between the lips.
Hold on to the h row. Add two dots and it becomes the b row. Add a small circle and it becomes the p row. Twenty of the marked kana you meet next come out of these five.

title.en: y, r, w, and the one that stands alone

unlocks.en: the whole basic table, all forty-six of it

en: The y row has three, not five: ya, yu, yo. yi and ye never existed as standard kana. The r row is full, and its sound sits between an English r, l and d.
The w row has two left: wa, and wo. The second is read o and is used for exactly one thing, which the particles rung covers.
Then there is n, which sits outside the grid entirely. It is the nasal from chapter 0, it takes a whole beat, and no standard Japanese word begins with it.

title.en: n is a beat, not a letter

en: It has no exercise here because there is nothing to choose between: there is one of it. It gets drilled inside every word that contains it, which is most of them.
This is why Gundam is four beats. ga, n, da, mu.

title.en: Two dots, and a small circle

unlocks.en: most native vocabulary, and the full sound inventory

title.en: Twenty-five more characters, and no new shapes

en: Two small dots voice the consonant. k becomes g, s becomes z, t becomes d, h becomes b. A small circle in the same corner turns h into p instead.
Nothing here is a new shape. It is the same forty-six with a mark, which is why this rung comes after all of them and not woven through.

title.en: The two you can almost ignore

en: The d row's i and u cells sound identical to the z row's, and the 1986 Cabinet Notice restricts them to two cases: a repeated sound in the same word, and a compound where the second word's consonant voiced.
So a word like inazuma takes the z row by default, and hanaji takes the d row because it is hana plus chi. Recognise them and move on.

unlocks.en: counting beats correctly, which is the difference between two words

en: An i-row kana followed by a small ya, yu or yo is one beat, not two. kyou, meaning today, is two beats. kiyou, meaning skillful, is three, and it is written with a full-size yo.
Size is the whole distinction. If the second character is small it joins the one before it; if it is full size it stands on its own.

title.en: Read the pair as one beat

unlocks.en: spelling a word you can already say, which is where hiragana stops being a decoder ring

en: The small tsu makes no sound. It holds the following consonant for one beat: saka is a hill, sakka is an author.

It never starts a word and never comes before a vowel. In native words it never precedes g, z, d, b or h. Loanwords are the licensed exception, which is exactly why beddo and baggu exist and look wrong.
Katakana writes a long vowel with a bar. Hiragana does not: it adds a vowel kana. a takes a, i takes i, u takes u, e takes e.
The o row is the one that trips people. The default is to add u, not another o: otousan, toudai, kyou, happyou.
The exception list is closed, short, and worth reading once. It is the words whose historical spelling had ho or wo after the o-row kana.

columns.en: Written with a second o, not with u

en: Twenty-two words, from the 1986 Cabinet Notice. Everything else with a long o takes u. There is no rule behind the list, only history, so it is a list and it is short on purpose.

title.en: And the e row does the same thing with i

en: The Notice's appendix writes a long e with i whether it is said as a long e or as ei: eiga, tokei, teinei, hei, mei, rei.
So tokei is spelled tokei and commonly said tokee. neesan and ee are counter-examples and sit in the main rule rather than the appendix.

title.en: u or a second o? (ō is a long o)

items.explain: おとうさん. The o row lengthens with u unless the word is on the exception list, and this one is not.
きょう. The default: a long o is written with u.
とうだい. Not on the exception list, so u.
はっぴょう. Not on the exception list, so u.

items.spelling: with a second o, it is on the exception list
items.explain: こおり. One of the twenty-two words whose long o is written with a second o.

items.spelling: with a second o, it is on the exception list
items.explain: おおきい. On the exception list: a second o, not u.

items.spelling: with a second o, it is on the exception list
items.explain: とおい. On the exception list: a second o, not u.

items.spelling: with a second o, it is on the exception list
items.explain: おおかみ. On the exception list: a second o, not u.
No small tsu, so the k is not held: sa-ka. With one it would be sakka, an author.
The small tsu holds the k for a beat: sa, small tsu, ka. Without it, saka is a hill.
The small yo rides on ki, so kyo is one beat, and the u makes it long: kyo-u, two beats.
A full-size yo is its own beat: ki-yo-u, three beats. The size of the yo is the whole difference from kyou.
The a row lengthens with a: ba-a. Say the long a or it becomes obasan, an aunt.
The i row lengthens with i: ji-i. Short, ojisan, is an uncle.
One of the few words whose long e is written with e rather than i.
Spelled with i, as the appendix writes a long e, and commonly said tokee.

title.en: The three that are read wrong on purpose

unlocks.en: reading a real sentence rather than a word list

en: Modern kana is otherwise one character to one sound. These three are not, and they are the only three.
ha is read wa when it marks the topic. he is read e when it marks a direction. wo is read o, and in contemporary Japanese it is used for nothing except marking the direct object.
The trap the Notice flags itself: a wa inside a word is a real wa, not the particle. Two of the commonest greetings you will meet, konnichiha and konbanha, end in the particle and are said with wa.

items.written: は in わたしはがくせいです
items.explain: This は marks the topic, so it is read wa: watashi wa gakusei desu, I am a student.
Inside a word は is a plain ha: hana, a flower. Only the particle is read wa.

items.written: へ in がっこうへいく
items.explain: This へ marks a direction, so it is read e: gakkou e iku, go to school.
Inside a word へ is a plain he: heya, a room.

items.written: を in ほんをよむ
items.explain: を marks the direct object and is read o: hon o yomu, read a book. It is used for nothing else.

items.written: は in こんにちは
items.explain: The greeting ends in the topic particle of a sentence nobody finishes, so it is wa: konnichiwa.
hai, yes, is a word, not a particle: plain ha.

items.written: は in こんばんは
items.explain: Same as konnichiwa: the greeting ends in the topic particle, so it is wa.

unlocks.en: reading at speed, which is where a near-miss stops being harmless

title.en: Learn them as contrasts, never one at a time

en: sa against ki: ki has two crossbars, sa has one.
nu against me: nu ends in a loop, me does not.
wa, re and ne: the tail decides. wa curves in, re hooks out, ne loops.
ru against ro: ru closes into a loop, ro does not.
The list of hiragana pairs is the researcher's own. No source enumerating them was found, which is worth knowing before you treat it as complete.

caption.en: ki. Two crossbars. The difference is the whole of it.

en: Every answer you give anywhere in this Book records how long it took, so speed is measured. Nothing here enforces it: there is no countdown and no round that fails you for being slow.
That is a gap rather than a decision, and it is named here rather than dressed up. What exists today is the measurement.

title.en: The last two drills are games, and they open in a frame
title.es: Los dos últimos ejercicios son juegos, y se abren en un marco

en: The rungs above drilled one row, or one rule, at a time. The last two drills here draw from the whole table at once, which is the only honest test of whether the kana is yours: reading a row inside the rung that taught it is not the same as reading a kana anywhere.

Both are games from quiz.neorgon.com running inside a frame on this page. The first shows a kana and asks for its sound, or shows a sound and asks for the kana, one at a time and picked per item; the second is a board of four kana against four romaji. Every answer is recorded here under this chapter's goal. Beside each frame there is an Open in Quiz link that opens the same round on its own page, so a frame that fails to load is never the end of the drill.
es: Los peldaños de arriba practicaron una fila, o una regla, cada vez. Los dos últimos ejercicios de aquí toman de toda la tabla a la vez, que es la única prueba honesta de si el kana ya es tuyo: leer una fila dentro del peldaño que la enseñó no es lo mismo que leer un kana en cualquier sitio.

Los dos son juegos de quiz.neorgon.com que se ejecutan dentro de un marco en esta página. El primero muestra un kana y pide su sonido, o muestra un sonido y pide el kana, de uno en uno y elegido por elemento; el segundo es un tablero de cuatro kana contra cuatro romaji. Cada respuesta se registra aquí bajo la meta de este capítulo. Junto a cada marco hay un enlace Abrir en Quiz que abre la misma ronda en su propia página, así que un marco que no carga nunca es el final del ejercicio.

en: Both start with a horizontal stroke and both curve away to the left underneath it. ki has two crossbars where sa has one.
Say them next to each other now: sa, ki, sa, ki. Learning them apart is what makes them fuse later.
The same body, and one of them ties a knot. nu finishes with a loop, me does not.
nu, me, nu, me.
Three characters, one left-hand stroke, and the whole difference is what the tail does. wa curves back in. re hooks out. ne loops.
This is the trio that costs beginners the most time, and it is the one where reading them as a set rather than one at a time actually pays.
ru closes into a loop at the bottom. ro stops.
Nothing is scored on these four pages. They are here to be looked at slowly, which is a different activity from being tested.
